## The Dwarf Kingdoms
## **Empire of Stone and Steel!**
_’Fool. Karaz Ankor is the foundation stone on which the whole world rests secure, the wall against which all dangers break, no matter what those Elves claim. It may be cracked in places, broken in others, but still it stands defiant. And if you value your lands and lives, manling, you‘ll pray on your scrawny knees to your Ancestors that never ends’._ 

— Stannok Stoutaxe to an Imperial officer, on the eve of the fourth battle for Garak’s Forge 

Beyond the Empire’s eastern borders, rising high above the world, are the endless jagged peaks of the Worlds Edge Mountains. In ancient days, deep below these snow-capped pinnacles, the Dwarfs hewed deep mines and mighty halls and built a kingdom of stone and steel — Karaz Ankor, the Everlasting Realm. 

Once, it was a thing of unmatched glory, a string of mighty holds ranging the length and breadth of the mountains, but so much has been lost to long years of suffering and woe. Nevertheless, like the Dwarfs themselves, Karaz Ankor endures, and woe betide any Dwarf-foe foolish enough to think its power spent. 

Karaz Ankor forever endeavors to reclaim what rightfully belongs to the Dwarfs and wreak vengeance against those who have offended them. 

A Dwarf ’s oath carries significant weight, and will be upheld by their family and descendants for as long as any of them draw breath. When the human Magnus called for aid against the forces of Chaos, it was the Dwarfs who answered first, honouring a pact made 2,000 years prior with Sigmar himself. 

The Dwarfs are an ancient civilisation, old when Humans still lived in caves and struggled to fend off beasts. They carry the weight of their history with pride and wear it openly no matter the company that they share. 

The Dwarfs are few, and their enemies more numerous than all the treasures in the fabled vaults of Karaz-aKarak. As a result, most Dawi, as the Dwarfs refer to themselves, possess a notable devotion to their own kind. Most are willing to sacrifice much so that their clan, honour, and hold can endure. A Dwarf ’s sense of honour and shame far surpasses that of the haughtiest Imperial Knight. Even minor insults are never forgotten, set in the stone-like mind of the slighted party. 

Dwarfs are a proud folk. A barely perceptible slight can incite a Dwarf to fury and they do not forget grudges. There is no word for forgiveness in Khazalid. If a person is so foolish to make an enemy of a Dwarf they will have an enemy for life, and the grudge may even carry down to their descendants. 

Dwarfs make records of the wrongs done to them, and every Dwarf hold has its own Book of Grudges. Within Karak-a-Karak, the capital of the Karaz Ankor and seat of the Dwarf High King, the Dammaz Kron is closely guarded. This is the Great Book of Grudges, a compilation of the most heartfelt and ancient grievances. Its first entries date back to the earliest history of the Dwarfs, a legacy of unrequited vengeance inherited from their ancestors. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

Karak Ungor and Karak Azgal are targets of Dwarf efforts to liberate them from the Orcs, Goblins, Skaven. The Dwarfs of Karaz Ankor are often willing to take on outsiders to help them — mercenaries are expendable, after all — but the gods help those who try to take souvenirs. 

With the long history of the Dwarfs, there are many lost holds, mines, and workshops for scholars to explore, treasure hunters to loot, or even for other Dwarfs to reclaim and restore. 

Not every adventure among the Dwarf holds is a hunt for treasure. Politics rears its ugly head among the Dawi, too. Once a unified realm, the western Karaks of the Grey and Black Mountains honour the High King, but do not submit to him. This has led to great grievances between them that have sometimes resulted in accusations of betrayal and the entering of grudges. 

Karaz Ankor’s great ally, the Empire, is still reeling from the events of the recent Turmoil. Its weakened state makes the Dwarf realm’s position less secure. 

The Empire’s engineering guilds and the more academically-minded Colleges of Magic covet the technological wonders of the Dwarfs. If the Dwarfs won’t share an invention, they are not above acquiring it by less honourable methods. Dwarfs of Karaz Ankor sent to recover a pilfered artefact would also be expected to make an example of the manlings who stole it. 

Rumours have reached Karaz-a-Karak of stirrings among the Vampire Counts of Sylvania and possible contact between them and the Chaos Dwarfs of the Dark Lands. With resources limited, the High King might need agents to investigate and find out the truth. 

Other Dwarf adventurers may find themselves acting as diplomats sent to settle a dispute between holds, or as dupes in a venture to reap untold riches at no small risk to themselves. 

Whatever approach the Gamemaster chooses to take, Karaz Ankor is a rich and exciting location with much to offer potential adventurers. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

## **Tarnished Glory: a History of the Dwarfs**
## **Introduction**
The Dwarfs are a truly ancient kin, whose origins reach back beyond the coming of Chaos to the world. It is a story sung in ballads, retold in sagas and recorded in vast halls of books made from precious metal or on stone tablets so old, they themselves are objects of veneration. The history of the Dwarfs — of the rise of Karaz Ankor, its near-total destruction, and its recovery — is so long that there are inevitable gaps where records have been lost. Recovery of lost knowledge is valued nearly as much as a new vein of gold. Considerable efforts are made to regain even a single loose page from a long lost journal. 

The story of the Dwarfs is a tale of glory, pride, disaster, struggle, and a stubborn endurance that equals the mountains themselves. 

## **Prehistory**
The Dwarfs believe their history begins with the awakening of their firstborn. Some of the oldest legends tell of a truly ancient being that forged the first Dwarf from earth, stone, and metal, in its workshop built deep beneath the Southlands. Others describe how their pantheon of gods came to be, carved by time from the rocks of the mountains, birthed by stone itself. Of these, the most prominent are Grungni, Grimnir and Valaya. They instilled in the Dwarfs a love of tradition, of the tried and tested, and a suspicion of the new. They charged the Dwarfs to go forth across the lands, to prosper and flourish under their guidance, and to ensure these values passed down to each new generation. 

It is said that under Grungni and Valaya’s guidance, they built the first Karak, a city both above and below ground, and called it Karak Zorn. This mighty bastion of a city grew both large and wealthy, and its armies stood steadfast in guarding it from any and all dangers. When Grungni commanded them to abandon their mighty home, it was met with both shock and confusion. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

Nevertheless they gathered kin and possessions and marched north along the spine of the Worlds Edge Mountains. They would eventually reach the Black Gulf. They began to found new Karaks, each location supposedly chosen by Grungni and Valaya. While some stayed behind to build these new holds, the rest continued northward. One group would turn away to the East, choosing to settle the Mountains of Mourn, while more pressed further north, as far as possible, creating holds in what would become Norsca. The majority, however, settled the ‘central ranges,’ from south of the Black Gulf to the edge of what is today Kislev. 

These vast new realms prospered under the guidance of Grungni, Valaya, and their children. They escaped disaster when Grungni warned of a forthcoming disaster the like of which the world had never seen. The colossal entrances to the holds were sealed shut and contact with the outside world cut. 

Soon after mighty explosions ripped both poles asunder and a cloud of mutating dust settled over the globe. 

It was for many long years — some say centuries — that the Dwarf holds remained isolated from both the world and each other. 

When the great gates once again opened, the Dawi found a world changed and filled with horrors. Contact was lost with the holds in the far north, and none knew what had happened to holds to the east. But concern for their kin had to wait as all the lands around Karaz Ankor had become infested with the hordes of Chaos. 

Led by Grungni’s brother, Grimnir the Slayer, Dwarf armies cleared the forests and river valleys west of Karaz Ankor when they reached the sea, where they discovered the Elves desperately defending their great port, _Sith Rionnasc’namishathir_ . Forming an alliance with the Elves, the combined armies of Karaz Ankor and Ulthuan cleared the Old World of Chaos, a struggle that took many years. Victory won, the two allies exchanged gifts and swore eternal friendship. 

A golden age had begun. 

## The Fate of the Norse Dwarfs
At the end of the Great Migration, several clans of Dwarfs pushed on beyond the World’s Edge Mountains and into the Giantshome range, which covered the eastern portion of what would become Norsca. Here they built several holds — Kraka Ravnsvake, Kraka Drak, and Kraka Dorden in the mountains, Kraka Ornsmotek beyond them. Clearing the lands of trolls, giants, and even dragons, the holds grew wealthy and their goods flowed south into the rest of Karaz Ankor. 

When Grungni’s warning arrived, the holds had barely time to seal their gates before the explosion at the pole and the waves of Chaos washed over the lands. For long years the holds remained closed against the horrors outside. When at last they opened their gates, they found the land in all directions awash with the horrors of Chaos. Brave parties of Dwarfs tried various ways to find a route south to reestablish contact with Karaz Ankor, but it was all for nought. Most never came back, dying or perhaps suffering a worse fate in the wilds. Those who did return were horribly mutated and had to be killed, while others had secretly turned to Chaos and only revealed their treachery after reentering the holds. The holds came to assume only they had survived and hunkered down for a long resistance. 

Eventually the tide of Chaos receded from the southern portions of Norsca, and the holds made contact with Humans settling the land, having crossed the sea in their primitive boats. At first glad to see others had survived the coming of Chaos, the Dwarfs traded with these tribes and, shaped by the harsh land they lived in, each took on characteristics of the other. Humans learned the secrets of brewing beer and mead, while Dawi art came to resemble that of the Norse tribes. 

But some Humans were vulnerable to the temptations of Chaos, and many of these newly arrived tribes eventually succumbed to the lure of the Dark Gods. Instead of trade, they would raid the Dwarfs, plundering their gold or for the simple joy of slaughter. Finally, the Norse Dwarfs were forced to take drastic action. They destroyed the trails leading to their holds and erected towering runestones barring entry to their lands and fortified their gates. Once again the Norse Dwarfs would isolate themselves. 

Yet there was a glimmer of hope in a time of seclusion. Human raiders who had crossed the southern sea spoke tales of the realms beyond opposed to Chaos. Among these, Dwarfs were said to dwell in mountain holds. Even as they sealed themselves against those drawn to Chaos, the Norse Dawi looked to a day when they might again see their kin. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

## The Quest for Karak Zorn
Scholars in both Karaz Ankor and across the human lands of the Old World have often speculated about Karak Zorn and its location. Dwarf records from the time of the Great Migration only exist as ancient ballads, folk tales passed from generation to generation or from crumbling tablets, chiselled many years after the volcanoes of the World’s Edge exploded. The difficulties of travel through these hostile lands make research and exploration almost impossible. Some even doubt that Karak Zorn is anything more than a myth, though one should never say that to a Dwarf’s face. 

The search for the lost city is an ideal goal for the ambitious. The greedy might dream of endless Dwarf gold, while covetous Gold Wizards can only imagine the magicaltechnological wonders left behind. A scholar would have his reputation made forever by proving its existence, while any Dwarf to uncover the ancestral home of their kind would want for nothing while they lived, and in death be recalled in sagas and ballads for so long as a single dwarf still lived beneath the mountains. 

It is up to the GM to decide what awaits the Characters there. Is the city empty? Haunted? Did a group of Dwarfs disobey Grungni to stay behind, and now their twisted descendants rule a mad realm? Have enemies of the Dawi taken it over, thus making it a matter of honour for Dwarf characters to clear it? 

It would be a challenge for even the most experienced Dwarf. 

## **The Age of Glory and Pride**
At the end of the War Against Chaos, Grungni and Valaya laid down their tools and, leaving the rulership of Karaz Ankor to their descendants, walked off into the depths of the earth, never to be seen again. 

They left behind a flourishing realm growing rich from the wealth of its mines. The holds that survived the wars prospered, and the Dwarfs founded new holds along the length of the World’s Edge wherever they discovered strikes of gold, gromril, and other precious metals and stones. Beyond the World’s Edge, ambitious Dwarfs began to explore the Grey, Black, and Vaults mountain chains, founding colonies of mines and forges in promising locations. It was at this time that the Great Underway, _‘Undgrim Ankor’_ , was built to connect all the holds of Karaz Ankor 

Trade with Elves added to Karaz Ankor’s prosperity. While the Dawi stuck to their mines and the slopes of the mountains, the Elves expanded from their coastal fortresses to explore the great rivers and forests of the continent. 

The Dwarfs in turn built a vast network of roads to connect their holds to the trading posts and colonies the Elves built along the rivers, and beyond them to the great ports of the coast. With their completion, trade flowed as never before. Dwarf craftsmen built formidable walls for the port of Sith Rionnasc’namishthir and an immense lighthouse for Tor Alessi, both of which still serve, though the sites are now known as Marienburg and L’Anguille. In return, the artists of Ulthuan crafted exquisite stained glass windows for the Great Hall of Karaz-a-Karak, which had become Karaz Ankor’s capital. 

Few thought this golden age could come to an end, but all things do. Unbeknownst to Karaz Ankor, a faction of Elves led by Malekith had rebelled against King Caledor, starting a civil war. To weaken their foes, Malekith’s ‘Dark Elves’ disguised themselves as Elves of Ulthuan and attacked trading parties from Karaz Ankor, stealing their goods and killing the Dwarfs. When High King Gotrek Starbreaker sent an embassy to Ulthuan to demand an explanation and compensation, the Elves instead themselves took offence and humiliated the ambassadors, shaving off their beards and sending them back in shame to Karaz Ankor. 

Unable to ignore or forgive the insult, Gotrek declared war on his former allies. This war, known by the Dwarfs as the War of Vengeance and by the Elves as the War of the Beard, became an existential war to see who would rule the continent. For over 400 years, war ravaged the lands of Dwarf and Elf, until the Elves had been pushed back to a few remaining coastal fortifications. The end came beneath the walls of Tor Alessi, where High King Gotrek met Phoenix King Caledor in single combat, slaying the Elf and taking his crown as a trophy. The Dwarfs had won, the Elves were forced to leave, and the armies of Karaz Ankor marched home, confident that they were masters of all they surveyed. 

Yet ruin was to follow. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

## **Time of Calamity**
Consumed by their need for vengeance against the Elves, the Dwarfs of Karaz Ankor failed to notice that others plotted their downfall. Deep in the bowels of the Earth, far below the holds and their mines, the vicious Skaven spent centuries working a great ritual with, some claim, the lost eastern clans who fell to Chaos at the time of the Great Disaster. 

The results of this ritual — or, by some accounts, uncontrolled arcane accident — were felt across the Old World, but nowhere more than in the World’s Edge Mountains, save perhaps Skavenblight itself. Having been granted only a handful of years to enjoy a hard-won peace, utter calamity was visited upon the Dwarfen holds. 

Quiescent since Grungni tamed them in a time of myth, all the volcanoes of the World’s Edge Mountains exploded at once. Fire, lava, and poisonous gas belched forth and poured down the slopes and through the valleys, destroying the surface settlements and burying the entrances to many holds. Powerful earthquakes accompanied the eruptions and were felt from the mountains to the sea. Untold numbers of Dwarfs died that day, and whole clans were made extinct. Then came the armies. 

As the last of the shocks settled and the Dwarfs began to assess the damage, armies of Skaven broke through into the tunnels beneath almost every hold, taking advantage of their weakened state. From the plains to the East, hordes of Orcs and Goblins swarmed up the valleys and into the holds, the gates of many broken and unmanned. 

The first to be lost was Karak Ungor, renamed Red Eye Mountain by Night Goblins, whose vile descendants would go on to hold it for millennia. It is perhaps because of this that this period became known as the Goblin Wars, though in fact, the Dwarfs faced Orcs, Trolls, Skaven, and countless other enemies. With the Underway breached and the surface unsafe, each hold found itself on its own in a desperate struggle to survive. Karaz Ankor teetered on the precipice of destruction. 

But it did not fall. Abandoning untenable holds in the eastern World’s Edge Mountains, survivors made their way to those that survived. The Dawi fought with a savagery and determination that made the War of Vengeance seem almost cordial, and in the deep tunnels and on the surface, the Dwarfs waged a war with no quarter given to defend their holds, to take back what was theirs. 

After decades of fighting, the front lines stabilised, communications and coordination with the surviving holds were restored. Though neither side was able to crush the other, the Dwarfs knew that time was against them. Their enemies were too numerous, they were unrelenting, and they would eventually overwhelm Karaz Ankor. If the Dwarfs were to survive this dire trial, they would not be able to do so alone. 

In the time since the primordial entry of Chaos to the world, a new people had moved into the forests and plains of what would become the Empire: Humans. Hunters, farmers, and crude workers of stone, they were a primitive people. However, where the Elves saw only barbarians, the Dwarfs saw potential. During the War of Vengeance, they traded with the tribes, teaching the Humans to work copper weapons and tools, in return for food. A friendship gradually grew between the peoples that became an alliance of common interest when the mountains erupted and the raucous swell of Orcs and Goblins poured across the passes and into the forests. Little did either know, however, how close that bond would become. 

## **The Great Sundering**
It was during the wars against the Orcs and Goblins that a faction among the Dwarfs came to despair not only of Karaz Ankor’s survival but that of the Dwarfs themselves. Made up of refugees from the fallen holds, these Dwarfs believed it was futile to try to retake their former homes — the Orcs and Goblins were too many and bred too fast, the Dawi too few, and increasingly, fewer. Though it meant abandoning the holds of their ancestors, these Dwarfs came to a momentous decision —they would leave Karaz Ankor and seek new homes in the mountains to the west. 

The High King and his Council denounced this as nothing less than treason, and a grudge naming every one of the ‘coward clans’ was entered into the Great Book. This did not deter them. They entered grudges against the High King in their own and departed. From their wanderings came the great holds of the Vaults, Black, and Grey mountains, such as Karak Hirn, Karak Izor, and Karak Norn. 

Relations between Karaz Ankor and the western karaks have since ranged from ‘cool’ to ‘rancorous’, with grudges laid and brought to often bitter conclusions, particularly when one or the other feels a lack of respect. The bonds among Dwarfs are usually strong, but while the Dwarf Kings of the western holds insist they respect the High King, they do not swear obedience, much to the High Kings’ annoyance. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

## **The Present Era**
The alliance proved a fruitful one. The Dwarfs supplied Sigmar’s people with steel and the secret of its forging. Kurgan also bequeathed Sigmar a mighty gift — Ghal Maraz, the Skull-Splitter, a rune hammer some say was forged by Smednir himself to be a sign of their people’s friendship. It would go on to become the symbol of the manling Emperors ever after. In return, Sigmar brought not only the Unberogens, but more and more of the great tribes of the plains and forests into the war putting the rampaging Orcs and Goblins to the sword. 

The nascent Empire and its Dwarfen allies would soon be tested. Drawn to warfare as moths to an open flame, a great horde of Orcs and Goblins swarmed through Black Fire Pass, aiming to destroy the realms of Dwarf and Man alike. In a battle whose outcome would echo through all the long years since, the allies crushed the invading Orcs and Goblins, driving them back into the deep forests and beyond the mountains. This moment of glorious victory led to the founding of the Empire and a new age for the Dwarfs. 

## Sigmar, Kurgan, and the Alliance of Honour
Kurgan Ironbeard, the renowned High King of Karaz Ankor, had faced death many times in his long life, yet the events that led to the Alliance of Honour truly made him believe his end had come. While leading a hunting party south of Karaz Ankor they were beset upon by a ferocious Orc warband. Displaying a cunning not common among the Orcs the ambush and surprise was total, and the intense fighting lasted mere minutes. Kurgan himself was captured and bound in irons. 

As the High King of Karaz Ankor must surely have prepared to meet his fate, an unexpected ally would come to his aid. A human named Sigmar, already renowned among his people, the Unberogens, rescued the High King of Karaz Ankor from the Orcs, and an unlikely but enduring alliance would be struck. For his assistance, Kurgan Ironbeard forged a bond of friendship that has existed between the Dwarfs and Sigmar’s heirs ever since, for Dwarfs never forget a debt, especially one incurred so long ago. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

## **The Age of Heroes**
The next thousand years was an era of renewed prosperity for Karaz Ankor. Many Dwarfs moved to the Empire’s settlements to help them build cities of stone and teach them the skills of true craftsmanship. With an increasingly stable Empire behind it, and the Orc and Goblin hordes for now no longer an existential threat, the Dwarf kings could concentrate on pushing back and recovering the lands they saw as ‘Grungni’s Bequest’. 

Many Dawi had their names entered in the Book of Remembrances, albeit often posthumously, for their efforts to rescue their peoples heritage. Foremost among them were Dorin Heldour and Katalin Kandoom of Karaz-a-Karak, veterans of Thori Gundrikson’s expeditions to the Black Water region in search of gromril. Seeking to win honour for themselves and their clans, they received the blessings of their clan elders and set out, following fragmentary clues that led them to the lost hold of Ekrund, called ‘Mount Bloodhorn’ by the Orcs who conquered it. 

There, sneaking past the Orcs and Goblins and other creatures lurking beneath the earth, they found the legendary Heartstone of Aldin Getgold, Ekrund’s greatest treasure. The Orcs discovered their trail, and a desperate fight followed before they could shake their pursuers and present the stone to High King Finn Sourscowl. 

But their greatest feat was the rescue of the Princes of Karaz Ankor. Captured by an Orc warband while on a hunting expedition in the south of Karaz Ankor, High King Finn’s two sons, Elmador and Oldor, were tossed into the dungeons of Black Crag, another of the lost holds. The Orc chief set back a message carved into the skin of their surviving guard promising the High King could have his sons back — piece by piece, a body part delivered each year on the anniversary of the Princes’s capture. The daring recovery of the heartstone fresh in his mind, the High King asked Dorin and Katalin to rescue his sons, bowing to them and swearing he would be forever in their debt. The friends accepted and set out immediately. Using a secret tunnel they discovered by searching old records in Karaz-a-Karak, they sneaked into Black Crag and slowly made their way to its ancient dungeons, barely avoiding discovery many times. There, in a stone-lined pit used for refuse, they found Elmador and Oldor barely alive, but still able to walk. Killing the guards and cutting the princes free, they made their way back toward the surface. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

As at Ekrund, however, the Orcs could not be fooled for long. Soon the pursuit began, and it seemed Dorin and Katalin had surely failed. But the Dwarfs had been crafty and prepared for this. One of the greatest sons of his mining clan, Katalin had created subtle weaknesses in the tunnels of Black Crag. Each time the Orcs threatened to catch them, he triggered a collapse that would block the tunnel. Nine times this happened, and nine times Orcs died from Dwarf craftiness. 

Eventually the small band escaped the tunnels of Black Crag and returned to Karaz Ankor. There the overjoyed High King kept his word, naming them champions and granting them each a tenth of his wealth. 

## **To Shield a Friend**
While Dwarfs had become an integral part of Imperial society as scholars, advisers, and craftsmen, there were those in the Empire, especially among its upper classes, who grew to resent the Dwarfs for their wealth and their seemingly patronising ways. Among the rulers of the Empire, there was a growing sentiment that Karaz Ankor treated the heirs of Sigmar as children, when it had been Sigmar who had saved their High King! Then came a time when two emperors, Ludwig the Fat and Boris Goldgather, decided the Dwarfs of the Empire should have to pay their fair share, which would happen to pay for the lavish corruption of their courts. They taxed the Dwarfs heavily, so much so that many were driven into ruin. Still, faced with insult after insult, the Dwarfs of the Empire and Karaz Ankor stood by their ancient oaths to Sigmar, time after time offering their advice and friendship to the manlings, only to have their beards tugged again. 

The Empire crashed in the year 1111 IC, when a virulent plague was followed by a Skaven invasion. The Dwarfs sealed their holds against the plague and battled the Skaven who breached their lower tunnels. When they reopened their great gates after many years, a devastating sight greeted them. The Humans under Emperor Mandred had beaten back the Skaven, but the Empire was a wreckage. Starvation and disease stalked the land, and the politics were in turmoil. It then came that Mandred fell at the hand of an assassin, and with that, a council tried to elect a new emperor, but failed. Civil war was the result, and the Dwarfs looked on in disbelief and deep disappointment as their once-powerful ally fragmented into a patchwork of squabbling princedoms. 

Still, an oath was an oath and, while the Humans were acting like fools, they were yet Sigmar’s people. The High King thus resolved that Karaz Ankor would keep watch over the Empire and protect it as best it could from its enemies until the Humans could gather the strength to raise themselves out of calamity. For the next thousand years, the Dawi did just that, with two great exceptions. 

The first came in 1707 IC when the Orcs and Goblins burst forth in a great Waaagh! Rising in the Badlands under the Orc Warlord Gorbad Ironclaw, the horde flooded through Black Fire Pass and other regions and invaded the Empire. The Dwarfs saw that meeting them in open battle would be suicidal, so they shut the great gates of their holds to wait it out. The devastation was Empire-wide, Averheim was sacked, Nuln was overrun and the province of Solland destroyed, the invasion culminating in the siege of Altdorf. 

Yet while Emperor Sigismund was slain, consumed by a wyvern, the city of Altdorf held. Denied their prize and beaten back by the Empire’s fierce defiance, the Waaagh! was forced back and Gorbad tried to retreat across Black Fire Pass. It was here that Karaz Ankor saw its chance. Led by the High King himself, the combined army of Karaz Ankor and the Black Mountains fell upon Gorbad’s forces in a battle that turned into a massacre. Though the fate of Gorbad himself is unknown, for the Dwarfs it was a debt repaid to both the Humans and the hated Orcs. 

The next was in the three Vampire Wars of the 21st and 22nd centuries. Because Sylvania was a province of the Empire, Karaz Ankor stayed out of the first war as much as possible as the vampire Count Vlad von Carstein launched a war to seize the Imperial throne. When the Grand Theogonist killed Vlad at the siege of Altdorf, the Dwarfs mistakenly thought the problem was solved. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

Vlad’s heir was the vampire Konrad von Carstein. He was interested in nothing but bloodshed and led his armies across the Empire in a feast of slaughter. Karaz Ankor could not stay neutral, for Konrad attacked the Dwarfs, raiding settlements loyal to Zhufbar. This led the King of Zhufbar to march forth with an army, where he met Konrad in battle. It was a disaster. The Dwarfs were annihilated, the King slain, and Konrad feasted on the blood of the Runesmiths. The Dwarfs had their revenge, however, in the battle of Grim Moor when Konrad was slain at last. As the Dwarf hero Grufbad restrained their common foe, the newly elevated Elector Count Helmar impaled the vampire with his Runefang. 

In the third and final Vampire War, the Dwarfs did not wait to become involved, allying with the Empire’s nobles to hunt down Mannfred, the latest of the von Carstein vampire counts, whose armies had ravaged the Empire. Trapping him in the Hel Fenn in 2145 IC, the forces of Karaz Ankor were crucial to forcing Mannfred to flee, whereupon he was cut down by the Elector Count of Stirland.Alliance Reborn 

If the Dwarfs hoped Humans would heed the lessons of the Vampire Wars and reunite their realm, they soon saw those hopes dashed. Once again the Empire fell to squabbling, petty wars, and further fragmentation. Karaz Ankor returned to tending to its own needs and keeping watch, its rulers certain they would endure this as they had all the other manling foolishness that had come before it. 

That mountain fell less than two centuries later. 

In 2302 IC, months of troubling signs and portents came true as the polar warp gates surged and the forces of Chaos waxed powerful. From the far north Asavar Kul, the Anointed of Chaos, led a huge army against Kislev and the lands of the Old World. The Tsar of Kislev sent out desperate messages for help, but the Elector counts of the fractured Empire only squabbled amongst themselves. Then Kislev’s field army was crushed at the Battle of the Lynsk, and Erengrad and Praag fell soon thereafter. In Karaz-a-Karak, knowing that only the combined forces of Karaz Ankor and the Empire had a chance to stop the Asavar Kul, High King Balun Alriksson felt despair grow in his heart. Though tempted to order the holds to shut their gates and hunker down as they did in the Great Disaster, he knew where his duty and honour lay. Laying aside his fear, he sent his son Prince Thorgrim Grudgebearer with a force of 1,000 Dwarfs to help the 

Tsar defend Kislev City and then turned himself to the defence of Karaz Ankor from the Orcs and Goblins besieging it. 

At this time, the manlings rallied behind an inspirational leader, a minor noble named Magnus, who called for all who were willing to fight to join him at the city of Talabheim. Balun felt amazement as his couriers brought reports of thousands, high-born and low, flocking to the manling’s banner. Even more shocking was the news that Ulthuan had sent help in the form of the wizard Teclis and two assistants, who would train manling magicians in the arts needed to defeat Asavar Kul’s Chaos Sorcerers. 

They were far from done. At a great battle before the gates of Kislev, the combined armies of the Empire, Kislev, Karaz Ankor, and the wizards trained by Teclis broke Kul’s forces and sent them fleeing back north. Recognising the key role Magnus had played and seeing a greatness in him no Human leader had shown in an age, Prince Thorgrim bowed before him on the field of battle and, in his father’s name, swore again the Oath of Kurgan, renewing the ancient alliance of Dwarf and Human. 

The friendship faced a sore test, however, when the Goblin Warlord Grom the Paunch of the Misty Mountain in 2410 IC led a massive Waaagh! through Black Fire Pass. The King of Karak Angazhar, Bragarik, led his army against Grom, but was defeated in a three-day battle that forced him to retreat to his hold. He appealed to High King Thorgrim for aid, and Thorgrim in turn sent a message to Emperor Dieter IV invoking their alliance while gathering his own forces. 

The reply shocked him. Dieter was facing a rebellion among the Elector Counts — one stoked by his own incompetence — and would send no help. Angered at this betrayal, Thorgrim entered Dieter and his kin into the Book of Grudges and ordered the holds to shut their gates. Grom’s force, gathering more and more Orcs and Goblins to it, was judged too great a threat to face alone. 

Though Grom and his army rampaged through the mountains, no Dwarf hold fell. Turning instead to ravage the Empire, he passed out of Karaz Ankor’s concern when he reached the Nordland coast, and sailed off into the Sea of Claws. Thorgrim, however, did not forget Dieter’s betrayal. Though Dieter had been deposed and replaced by the far sturdier Wilhelm III, the Dwarfs still question to this day just how much they can rely on the manlings.

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

## **Adventuring in the Dwarf Realms**
While extensive trade exists between the Dwarf holds and the Empire — as well as Bretonnia, Tilea, and even Estalia — travel within Karaz Ankor and the other Dwarf Kingdoms is not a simple matter. Thousands of years of hard experience have made most Dawi wary of outsiders entering their realms and, especially, the holds themselves. Travel in the mountains is dangerous, for The Dwarf Kingdoms are lands under siege, even in the best of times. Trolls, Orcs, Goblins, bandits, and even illegal miners (whom the Dwarfs treat as thieves) make every journey a hazardous one. This section provides a brief guide for those travelling to them. Though centred on Karaz Ankor, it applies to other Dwarf realms, as well. 

## **On the Road**
In the heyday of friendship between Elf and Dwarf, after the War Against Chaos, the Dwarfs became great roadbuilders. From the holds of Karaz Ankor to the Elves living along the sea, roads of dressed stone crisscrossed the land. Along these travelled trade caravans and messengers and, where there were no Elf settlements. The Dwarfs built way-stations where travellers could safely rest. The road system was one of the wonders of the age. 

But time and catastrophe take their toll, and little of it remains. Many have become the main roads of the Empire, but covered by manling work, or lost amidst the forests. Some have fallen out of use and into ruin, as the holds they led to have been lost to Orcs, Goblins or worse. Few travel them now, other than to make war. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

Others are still in use, heading up river valleys and mountain passes to the remaining holds, but, outside the Dwarf realm’s boundaries, they are indifferently maintained, at least by Dwarf standards. 

The most famous of these is the Old Dwarf Road, that runs from Karaz-a-Karak to Talabheim. Recognizing the wealth it brings, the rulers of Averland and Talabecland have agreed with the High King to contribute to its upkeep, providing money and labour for road maintenance in their lands — with Dwarf inspection — making the entire road relatively easy to travel. Fortified inns and regular Roadwarden patrols provide rest and security from the border to Talabheim. 

Outside Karaz Ankor, other well-known roads are the King’s Highway, leading from Ubersreik to Karak Azgaraz and beyond to Bretonnia, and the Montdidier Pass, which runs past Kazad Elgazund, the mines and trading post owned by Karak Ziflin. The Dwarfking of Karak Ziflin keeps a close eye on this road, for the way west to Bretonnia travels perilously close to the Loren Forest and the Elves who live there. Abandoned roads include the Silver Way, which leads east from Karaz-aKarak to the lost hold at Mount Silverspear, and Mad Dog Pass, which is now little more than an invasion route for marauding Orcs and Goblins from the Dark lands to the Border Princes and beyond. 

## **Across the Frontier**
Visitors to Karaz Ankor do not have a clear path to a Dwarf hold’s gates. Far from it. Forever concerned about security, the Dawi want to know a traveller’s business and background, and the answers determine where and how far they are allowed to go. Their first encounter along the road is often with a Dwarf fortified inn, which also functions as a border checkpoint and trading post. Travellers found off the road are directed to the trading post and treated with a great deal of suspicion. 

Along the Old Dwarf Road, about a half day’s march past the border where the road enters a narrow valley, sits the Karaz Ankor Inn and Trade House, currently managed by Izar Grimboldsson, a Dwarf merchant whose clan holds the hereditary right to run the post. Serving him are ten Dwarfs, all members of the same clan, who work at the hold and provide security for it. Izar and his assistant buy and sell goods with traders who have no need to go further, and the post provides a reinforced warehouse to store both Dwarf goods and those of visiting traders. Izar’s Trade House has a few rooms to rent and stables for horses and mules, but large caravans are expected to camp outside and seek shelter in the post at the first sign of trouble. 

Travellers who need to go further must obtain a Writ of Passage, and the only way to get one is through a lengthy interview with Snorri Bograz, a Runescribe on his first assignment. Mindful of his duties to the point of officiousness, Snorri personally questions each member of a party individually about their business, their intentions, their prior travels, and their ancestors. Unsatisfactory answers will result in curt refusal, and many travellers have learned to dread hearing Snorri raise one final question just when they thought the interview was over. If Snorri approves, then the visitor receives a Writ of Passage. Snorri is also scrupulously honest, as the last manling who tried to bribe him found out, much to his pain. 

## **The Writ of Passage**
Visitors permitted to travel within Karaz Ankor receive rune-enchanted writs of travel and passage that briefly state the bearer’s business, destination, and where they are allowed to go. These documents must be presented on demand, such as when encountering a patrol of Dwarf Rangers. Failure to do so can lead to immediate expulsion from Karaz Ankor, or even arrest on suspicion should the Dawi have any reason to think the travellers are up to anything nefarious. Some Dwarf officials take particular delight in harassing Elves. 

A typical Writ of Passage is made of thin sheets of metal between leather binding. The required information is engraved on the metal by a Runescribe in both Khazalid and Reikspiel, though Runescribes annoyed with a traveller have been known to add runes in Khazalid commenting on the bearer’s characteristics and even suggesting they be given a hard time. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

Three metals are commonly used for these documents. Copper is the lowest level and indicates the bearer is allowed to travel along the road and visit the town outside a hold, but only for a specified purpose and they may not enter the hold itself. Silver allows greater leeway to the bearer, granting permission to visit several sites, stay an indefinite length of time, and even enter the hold, itself, but only if they can convince the gate officials they have good reason, such as having business with royal or clan officials. Gold is the highest level, only granted to travellers who can show they are on urgent business vital to the Dawi’s interests. It allows the bearer to travel where they wish, grants them unquestioned entry to the hold, and opens the door to the highest officials, including the Dwarf king. 

Gold documents are typically granted only to upper nobility, their ambassadors, or those who have earned the title ‘Dwarf Friend’. The Dwarfs take these matters so seriously, that the forgery of one means branding and expulsion. Forging a gold Writ of Passage, however, is a capital offence. 

## **Within the Realm**
Once past the border post, whether legally or by finding a sneaky way around it, travellers enter a realm familiar in some ways, alien in others, and with wonders so ancient that it makes the finest districts of the cities of men look like slums in comparison. 

## **Other Settlements**
Though a realm is named for its hold, that is not the only place where Dwarfs live. All holds have dependent mines away from the main hold, where clans extract valuable metals, minerals, and gemstones from distant veins. These tend to be isolated and away from the main routes, rarely receiving non-Dwarf visitors and even more rarely giving a warm welcome to those who do call. The entrance to the mine is often hidden behind a fortified blockhouse, and the Dwarfs keep enough supplies to withstand a siege of weeks. Kazad Urkbavak near Karaz-a-Karak is one of the more well-known. 

There are also small clanholds. More than just mines, these are the hereditary holdings of clans who owe fealty to the local Dwarfking. Perhaps they work mines, or maybe operate workshops wherein they can practise their craft in peace, away from the stifling supervision of craft elders in the main hold. Or maybe a grudge with another clan has led them to separate themselves. Regardless, these clans hold their land in return for service, often guarding a little-used pass or path, with the obligation to warn the main of danger and delay it as long as possible. These are most common on the eastern frontier of Karaz Ankor, where they keep watch for a return of the Orc and Goblin hordes. 

## **Dwarf Rangers**
The Dwarfs do not sit back passively, waiting for danger to come. The defence of Karaz Ankor and other realms requires an active watch for troublemakers. Thus evolved the rangers, Dwarf specialist troops trained to spend long periods in the wilderness above ground. Working alone or in small groups, they patrol the mountains looking for anyone or anything who doesn’t belong there — Orcs, Goblins, Trolls, mutants, Human bandits, and those who would rob the treasures of the lost holds. Winter is no obstacle to the rangers, who are trained to travel and fight on skis. The Dwarf rangers have been known to provide rescue work, helping travellers lost in the mountains and in danger of freezing, each patrol carrying a small keg to give them warmth and stoke a fiery spirit. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

## Humans Among Dwarfs
One aspect of the Dwarf realms that often puzzles first-time visitors is the Human residents. These are not Imperial citizens living among the Dwarfs as traders, rather they are Human subjects of the Dwarf king. They are citizens of the hold with full rights and are subject to Dawi Law. In return for the Dwarf king’s protection, they provide farming and herding services, act as intermediaries with visiting nonDwarfs, and serve in the hold’s armed forces. 

Lost travellers have even encountered Ranger patrols that were mixed Dawi and Human subjects who live within a Dwarf realm. While most often encountered in the trade towns outside a hold, there are Humanvillages in the mountains on the slopes and by lakes that provide food to nearby holds, the most well-known being Domatburg, Mont Glace, and Hochstadt, all in the Vaults. 

These Human allies had their origins in an ancient people, the Belthani, who inhabited the plains and forests before the coming of the Unberogens and the other tribes. Peaceful farmers and pastoralists, they befriended the Dawi during the War of Vengeance, providing supplies in return for copper tools. 

In the many long years that followed they could not resist the advance of these new tribes,  and faced destruction in a war they were incapable of fighting. At last, the Dwarfs took pity on them and their then High King,Logan Proudbeard,  offered them protection in return for service. Their descendants have never forgotten this kindness. 

## **Wonders and Dangers**
Without a doubt, travel within the mountains is dangerous, and one leaves the main roads only cautiously, knowing that great peril awaits. Not all dangers come from predators or monsters. The World’s Edge Mountains, home to Karaz Ankor, are taller than any in the world, and carved deep with hidden valleys. Narrow trails skirt the sides of the mountains, not even wide enough for one person to walk in comfort.  High winds and sudden storms threaten to sweep the unfortunate off their feet and to their doom, while an avalanche could sweep all away in a few terrifying moments. 

But, for all its risks, the Dwarf Kingdoms hold marvels to make even the most jaded Imperial scholar’s jaw drop. Foremost among these are the skybridges, fabulous arched spans that stretch between mountain peaks easing (as the Dwarfs see it) travel between the holds. Products of the Golden Age after the War Against Chaos, some bridges are wide enough for three carts to pass comfortably sideby-side, while others leave barely enough room for one person to walk. Many have walls to guard against the high winds that could send a traveller hurtling down into deep chasms, but others are just open, exposed roads. Almost all have handrails, but the Dwarfs consider it a mark of courage not to use them and will sometimes put non-Humans to the test. There are also rumours that the bridges have powerful runes carved into them, ready to bring down the span at a Runemaster’s command, should an enemy be about to capture them. The most well-known to Reiklanders are the three sky-bridges of Karak Azgaraz — Barakdokerinnalad, Dalgrongi, and Unzaled — which are found on the King’s Highway west of Ubersreik. 

## No Further
In Karaz Ankor, the King’s Highway once spanned every peak from Karaz-a-Karak to the great mines at Mount Silverspear, the bridge wide enough to let carts pass side by side as they went back and forth. When the volcanoes erupted and Mount Silverspear fell to the Goblins. However, that same road provided an open way to Karaz-a-Karak. As a horde of wolfriders raced across, the Runemaster Khelezh sacrificed himself to crash the span, sending both himself and the Goblin horde to their deaths. To this day, the broken sky-bridge stands as a reminder to all Dawi that they themselves might one day have to pay the ultimate price. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

## **Karaz Ankor Today**
The Dwarf Empire still reigns supreme in the World’s Edge Mountains, though, to the perceptive visitor, that supremacy looks cracked and battered. While High King Thorgrim Grudgebearer sits in grim majesty on the Throne of Power, he hides within him concerns for the future. Will Chaos surge again, bringing with it hordes of Orcs, Goblins and Trolls — and worse? Can the lands of Men, especially the Empire, be relied on in a crisis? And what of the Dawi, themselves? Often flawed by greed and pride, the Dwarfs contain within themselves the seeds of their own downfall. 

## **Mountain Life.**
Karaz Ankor and the World’s Edge Mountains are synonymous in the minds of most people and, indeed, the Dwarf realm at its height ruled the chain from its northern foothills deep into the lands of the south. It claimed suzerainty over the mountain holds of Norsca and the eastern holds of the Mountains of Mourn. 

Even after thousands of years of war and upheaval, it is a vast realm. 

Kazador is not alone in his determination, for the vast majority of Dawi refuse to abandon the mountains,in spite of the gradual, grinding losses that most know will someday end in Karaz Ankor’s downfall. For most the idea of leaving the mountains is unthinkable, as alien as the idea of an Elf doing manual labour. The mountains were Grungni’s bequest to the Dwarfs, their source of wealth and their shelter in the Great Disaster. For a species often outnumbered, the rough terrain of the mountains helped them fight off far more numerous invaders, amounting to a weapon as important as any technology. 

And, as time and generations passed, the prospect of abandoning the tombs of their ancestors in the face of anything less than overwhelming force became unthinkable, a shame that even the Slayer’s Path might not expunge. For the Dwarfs of Karaz Ankor, the mountains are home, they are Karaz Ankor, they are the Dwarfs, themselves. 

## **Politics**
While Karaz Ankor puts forth an image of unity and purpose to outsiders, its politics are as complicated and fraught as any Human realm’s, and often far more obtuse. 

## **Within Karaz Ankor**
In the far north, Karaz Ankor officially begins in the mountains above the Belyevorota Pass, where Karak Vlag had close relations with the Tsars of Kislev. But Karak Vlag fell in the Incursion of Chaos, and the Dwarfs refuse to speak casually of its fate out of shame and horror. Now, Karak Kadrin is the last northern hold, though the High King bitterly resists any attempts by the Tsars to claim the mountains around Belyevorota, even if no Dawi currently live there. 

Though once the empire extended south past the junction with the Mountains of Mourn, the southernmost remaining hold is Karak Azul. Though wealthy from its great iron mines, it sits almost isolated by the Orc, Goblin, and Skaven infested ruins of Karak Azgal to the south and contested Karak Eight Peaks to the north. With the roads both below and above the ground too dangerous for caravans to risk, trade goes instead to Barak Varr, whence it moves on by land through the Border Princes, or by sea. In spite of its isolated, precarious position, its aged King, Kazador, rejects abandoning its wealth. Having lost his family, he refuses to lose his heritage, too. 

From its foundation through the Golden Age, Karaz Ankor was a unitary realm, in which the rule of the High King of Karaz-A-Karak was supreme. This seemed natural, as the Founder and first ruler was himself a god, Grungni, and his heirs carried great authority. While the individual holds had their own leaders, these were clearly sub-kings who ruled at the High King’s pleasure. 

But the volcanic eruptions and invasions that marked the end of the age also put an end to this direct rule. The sundering of the Underway and the dangers of the surface ways left the holds on their own for many years. Forced to fight for survival with almost no help from outside, few surviving holds were willing to return to the way things were. Indeed, many bore grudges, justified or not, against Karaz-a-Karak for failing to protect them. 

In the end, the need for unity against their enemies and their instinctive reverence for tradition drove the Dawi to reach a compromise. The kings of each surviving hold would become sovereign in their own right, but would owe loyalty to the High King and answer his call to arms. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

And that same respect for the Throne of Power would mean that the High king’s wishes carried weight in the other holds, even if they were rarely commands. In fact, an Imperial scholar once observed to the High King that the structure of Karaz Ankor is not that different from that of the Empire… which promptly saw him expelled and banned from reentry. 

Within a hold, while the Dwarfking’s word is law, he is also obliged to consult with a Council of Elders. Usually composed of the heads of the noble clans, the chief priests of Grungni and Valaya, the head of the Engineers Clan, the senior Loremaster, and those royal officials deemed essential, their duty is to render their best advice to their king. While under no obligation to accept this advice, the lack of a convincing explanation for a refusal to do so can lead to discord within the hold and even grudges. 

## Slayers in Karaz Ankor
Spiritual descendants of Grimnir, the First Slayer, hold an odd place in the politics of the Dwarf Empire. Burdened with a shame so great it can only be expiated by death in battle, Slayers are often regarded as unpredictably violent, even mad by other Dawi, yet also held in an almost religious awe. The idea that a Slayer has done something so disgraceful that they have, in essence, cut themself off from their clan and imposed a death sentence on themself can shake anyone who thinks about it to their core. And the Dwarfs try not to think about it. They simply point them toward the nearest enemies and try to stay out of their way. 

Dwarfs breathed a sigh of relief, therefore, when King Baragor in -650 IC consecrated the great shrine to Grimnir in Karak Kadrin. The shrine attracted Slayers from across all the realms of the Dwarfs, giving them a place where they were honoured without being feared. From their fellows and the priests of Grimnir, they learn to focus their rage to enable them to at least minimally function in society. 

As King of the Slayers, the King of Karak Kadrin not only rules over his own hold, but has the right also to sit on the Council of Elders of the High King, where he speaks for all Dwarfs who seek redemption through death. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

## **Beyond the Kingdom**
Much as it wishes the outside world would leave it alone, Karaz Ankor has vital interests that require it to interact with the lands around it. 

## **The Norse Dwarfs**
Cut off from Karaz Ankor for nearly 7,000 years after the Great Disaster and the Coming of Chaos, the Dawi of the greatest of the remaining holds in the Giantshome Mountains, Kraka Ravnsvake, reestablished contact with their southerly kin on hearing of their existence from Erengrad traders in 2290 IC. Welcomed as lost brothers when they knocked at the gates of Karak Vlag, the two parties quickly established a prosperous trading partnership — furs and strong (even for a Dwarf) beer from Kraka Ravnsvake, high-quality metal tools and weapons from Karaz Ankor. Slayers from the Old World and the Western holds passed through the Norscan holds on their way north, looking for a glorious death. It looked as if the realms would be reunited at long last. 

The Chaos Incursion of 2302 IC ruined all that. While the hordes of Asavar Kul invaded Kislev, put Praag and Erengrad to the sword, and conquered Karak Vlag, the Norse Dwarfs did what they could to aid their trading partners and kin. Sortieing from their underground ports, their ships harassed the coastal flanks of the Horde of Chaos and prevented their raiders from reaching the vulnerable coast of the Empire. With the war’s end, the new High King, Thorgrim, thought it time to make the reunification formal. 

The Dawi of Kraka Ravnsvake had other thoughts. 

A messenger arrived at Kraka Ravnsvake from Karaza-Karak with a proclamation from Thorgrim. He commanded King Haarkon Vikramsson and his Queen, Inga Ottarsdottir, present themselves before the Throne of Power to swear their allegiance and obedience, as was done in the days of the High Kings before the Coming of Chaos. When the envoy was done reading the proclamation, Haarkon sat for long moments in silence before issuing this reply. 

Upon receiving word of this, Thorgrim was furious, but there was little he could do. Karaz Ankor needed all the allies it could get, and the joy at finding their lost kinsmen had been so great, none could bear the idea of a break in relations again. Also, an attempt to impose Karaz Ankor’s authority could now only be done by force, which would ruin relations with the western holds, too great a price to pay. So Thorgrim agreed, and the Norse holds remain allied but independent to this day. 

## **The Western Holds**
Born of the exodus from Karaz Ankor of Dwarfs dispossessed from its fallen holds and despairing of ever returning, the holds of the Vaults, Black, and Grey mountains are a regular irritant for the High King. At their formation, the High King condemned them as cowards and entered grudges against each and every one, which the western holds returned with grudges of their own.  This situation lasted for a thousand years, and they avoided war with each other only because of Karaz Ankor’s pressing need to fight Orcs, Goblins and Skaven. 

Eventually the pressure of war led the High King to attempt reconciliation. He tore out the relevant pages in his Book of Grudges and sent them to the Dwarfkings of the western holds with a message that all grudges were withdrawn. He declared the Dawi of the western mountains were again welcome in Karaz Ankor and expressed the hope that reconciliation would lead to their reunion with Karaz Ankor — as well as their warriors and gold. 

Moved by this gesture and the innate urge of all Dwarfs to stick together, the western Dwarfkings in turn tore out their own pages and sent them to Karaz-a-Karak, thus ending the schism. They would not, however, rejoin Karaz Ankor, nor would they do more than swear allegiance — any idea of fealty or subordination was left conspicuously out. The High Kings grumble and accept this arrangement, however, because of the needs of war, and the western holds’ willingness to provide aid. 

Contrary to what Thorgrim must have expected, Haarkon was not eager to offer his fealty. Rather, he proclaimed that he would swear obedience only to the true High King, that being Grungni himself. 

XI **I** XV **I** XI **I** 

## **The Empire**
Karaz Ankor’s most important relations are with the Empire. It is the crucial source for trade, both imports of food and revenue from the export of Dwarf craft goods. The Empire is also a key source for mercenaries, whose presence fills out the ranks of the Dwarf holds’ armies, especially the cavalry so important to battles on the surface. And, in times of great crisis, High King Thorgrim knows from bitter experience in Kislev that Karaz Ankor’s chances of survival are much better when the Empire’s armies and wizards take the field. 

To make sure, then, that relations with the Imperial Court stay strong, Karaz Ankor maintains an embassy in Altdorf, led by his kinsman, Mordin Harginsson ( **Altdorf** , page 19). Young and brash for such an important post, Harginsson claims precedence over the ambassadors from Karak Norn and Karak Azgaraz, much to their annoyance. He is also patronising toward the Dwarfs of Altdorf, reflecting the prejudice many of Karaz Ankor feel toward Dwarfs who have chosen to live among Humans. Harginsson’s abrasive ways have led to quiet complaints both to Duchess Ullana Veltan, High Chamberlain of the Seal ( **Altdorf** , page 20), and to Karaz-a-Karak, but it remains to be seen if Thorgrim will replace him. 

Within the Empire, Karaz Ankor is most concerned with affairs in the provinces bordering it, and so it has sent legates to the courts of Averland, Ostland, and Ostermark, though the post in Sylvania remains empty after the disappearance of the last legate. While representing Karaz Ankor’s interests and those of the local Dwarfs when asked, these diplomats are careful not to step on the beard of the Ambassador in Altdorf, nor to upset the Imperial Court in their dealings with provincial rulers. 

## **Other Realms**
None of the other manling lands approach the importance of the Empire to Karaz Ankor, save for two: Kislev and the Border Princes. With the last Incursion of Chaos always in the back of his mind, Thorgrim has not only sent an ambassador to Kislev City, but also a guard of 100 veteran Dwarf warriors to bolster its defences. He is also considering a gift of artillery to guard its walls. 

The chaos of the Border Princes raises risks for southern Karaz Ankor, but Thorgrim leaves affairs there to King Zamnil Grundisson of Barak Varr, whose commercial contacts along the Black Gulf provide excellent sources of information. 

Relations with the other manling lands are left to the Dwarf holds nearest them, mostly because Thorgrim has enough to deal with as well as keep the western holds from feeling insulted by Karaz Ankor’s meddling. The House of Fooger has the contract to represent the Dwarf Empire’s interests in Marienburg. Rumours persist that, in spite of the disdain Karaz Ankor may feel toward flatlander Dawi, the High King is not too proud to take the occasional — and confidential — loan from Arkat Fooger to keep his armies in the field. 

Though no direct relations exist between Ulthuan and Karaz-a-Karak, when contact or negotiations seem prudent, these matters are handled behind closed doors between the Ambassador of Karaz Ankor, and Daendra Stillwater ( **Altdorf** , page 18). Stillwater, it is rumoured, finds Ambassador Harginsson’s visits about as welcome as a fly in her wine.
